title: The bhog
hook: the close of a complete reading, with the last pages, Anand and Ardas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sehaj path: the whole Granth in order, at a walking pace, named for poise. Your line was your own pace. Where did you put your bookmark? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

The room has been quiet for days, one reader's voice after another. Now it's filling up. Cousins arrive from across town. Somebody's grandmother is helped to a spot near the front. Children are hushed and sat down. The reader is close to the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and everyone has come to hear the last pages together. A whole reading, whether it was unbroken or slow, is about to close. How it closes has a name, and a shape, and the shape carries its own teaching.
screen: `THE ROOM FILLS UP.` → `THE LAST PAGES, TOGETHER.` → `HOW IT CLOSES HAS A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: The word is bhog. In Sikh use, it names the close of a complete reading of the Granth. First come the last pages. Near the very end is a short passage called the Mundavani, the seal, by Guru Arjan. In paraphrase: in this platter three things have been placed, truth, contentment and contemplation, and with them the Name, the support of all; whoever eats of it, whoever enjoys it, is saved. So the Granth ends by describing itself as a meal. Everything read over those days turns out to have been a plate set before the sangat. Communities differ on where the reading stops, whether at the Mundavani or carrying on through the Ragmala that follows it, and the code notes that difference and leaves it to custom. Then Anand Sahib is sung, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss. Anand means bliss, and the reading closes not with a sigh of relief but with joy. Then everyone stands for the Ardas, the prayer that remembers the Gurus and asks for the Guru's grace, and the reading is offered up. A hukam is taken, and karah prashad, the sweet offering, is shared, which is tomorrow's story. Look at what the bhog refuses to do. It doesn't let the last page just run out, the way a phone call can just drop. It gathers people. It names what was received. It gives thanks out loud. It asks forgiveness for any mistake in the reading. Then it feeds everyone. A long reading ends not by stopping but by being completed. End well.
screen: `BHOG: THE CLOSE OF A READING.` · `THE MUNDAVANI'S PLATTER.` · `ANAND SAHIB, THE SONG OF BLISS.` · `THE ARDAS, THEN A SHARED OFFERING.` · then, large: `END WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of an ending well done. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that ended well: a goodbye at an airport, a last day at a job, a hard conversation that closed with a hug, a life honored at a funeral. What made it a good ending? Who was there? Was something said out loud? Then think of something in your own life that's ending soon, small or large. What would it take to end it well? Rest with that until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Bhog. The close of a complete reading: the last pages, Anand Sahib and the Ardas, and then a shared offering. Today's word.
Your line: end well. Today, close one thing on purpose, a task, a visit, a call, with a word of thanks out loud before it's over. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: At a bhog, family and sangat gather for the final pages of the Guru Granth Sahib; Anand Sahib is sung, the Ardas is said standing, a hukam is taken and karah prashad is shared, often followed by a meal in the langar.
